flowers.name: ★ State Flower: White Pine Cone and Tassel
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full plant entry for ecological details.
flowers.description: Maine's state flower is actually the cone and tassel of the Eastern White Pine — unique among state flowers.

flowers.name: Lupine
flowers.wildlife: Host plant for Karner Blue butterfly. Nitrogen fixer.
flowers.description: Tall spikes of purple-blue flowers are iconic along Maine roadsides and fields in late spring. Wild lupine is the only host plant for the endangered Karner Blue butterfly. Thrives in sandy, poor, acidic soils where little else grows.

flowers.name: Bunchberry
flowers.wildlife: Berries eaten by 37+ species of birds. Ground-covering woodland plant.
flowers.description: Miniature dogwood ground cover with white flower bracts and bright red berry clusters. Essential woodland floor plant in Maine's boreal forests. Spreads slowly to form carpets in acidic, shaded conditions.

flowers.name: Wild Blue Flag Iris
flowers.wildlife: Attracts native bumblebees. Important for wetland pollinators.
flowers.description: Striking blue-violet iris native to Maine's wetlands, pond margins, and bogs. Tolerates standing water. The official wildflower of Quebec and a beloved native throughout eastern boreal regions.

flowers.name: Fireweed
flowers.wildlife: Major nectar source for bees. Important for honey production in northern Maine.
flowers.description: Tall magenta flower spires that colonize disturbed ground, clearcuts, and post-fire areas. One of the first plants to return after forest disturbance. Blooms progress upward on the spike — when bloom reaches the top, summer is nearly over.

flowers.name: Pitcher Plant
flowers.wildlife: Carnivorous — traps insects. Unique bog ecosystem plant.
flowers.description: Maine's carnivorous bog plant — hollow pitcher-shaped leaves trap rainwater and drown insects to extract nutrients from nutrient-poor bog water. The reddish nodding flowers are pollinated by bumblebees. State flower of Newfoundland.

flowers.name: Trillium
flowers.wildlife: Seeds dispersed by ants (myrmecochory). Slow-growing forest wildflower.
flowers.description: Deep red-maroon three-petaled wildflower of rich deciduous forest floors. Takes 7+ years to bloom from seed. Never pick — removal kills the plant. Entire plant arrangement is in threes (petals, sepals, leaves). Beloved spring ephemeral.

flowers.name: Wild Blueberry
flowers.wildlife: Over 40 bird species eat berries. Critical bear food. Supports native bees.
flowers.description: Maine's most economically important native plant — wild blueberry barrens cover thousands of acres of Washington County. Spreads by rhizome to form dense low mats. Produces small intensely flavored berries far superior in antioxidants to cultivated varieties. Requires acidic rocky soil with low nutrients.

flowers.name: Steeplebush
flowers.habitat: Wet meadows, pond margins, stream banks
flowers.wildlife: Attracts native bees and butterflies. Important wetland shrub.
flowers.description: Deep pink flower spikes rising above woolly-leaved stems in Maine's wet meadows and pond margins. One of the most beautiful native shrubs for moist sites. Blooms in mid-summer when most other shrubs have finished. The dense woolly underside of leaves is distinctive.

flowers.name: Sheep Laurel
flowers.wildlife: Bee plant. Toxic to livestock.
flowers.description: Low-growing native shrub with clusters of deep pink flowers in acidic meadows and bogs — related to mountain laurel but smaller and with more intense flower color. Toxic to sheep and cattle — hence the name. Found throughout Maine's rocky coastal barrens alongside blueberries and Labrador tea.

flowers.name: Meadowsweet
flowers.habitat: Wet meadows, stream banks, bog edges
flowers.wildlife: Attracts native bees and small butterflies.
flowers.description: Native shrub with plumes of tiny white flowers in wet meadows and along stream banks throughout Maine. One of the most common plants of Maine's old farmland going back to pasture — indicates formerly grazed ground. Provides structure and late-season bloom in wetland plant communities.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Purple Lilac
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full plant entry for ecological details.
flowers.description: Introduced from Europe but deeply embedded in New Hampshire's spring landscape.

flowers.name: Pink Lady's Slipper
flowers.wildlife: Pollinated by bumblebees — deceptive pollination (no nectar offered).
flowers.description: New Hampshire's most celebrated wildflower — a native orchid that lives in the acidic soil beneath pines. Takes 10–17 years to bloom from seed. Has a specific mycorrhizal fungus relationship — never transplant. One of the most photogenic native wildflowers of the Northeast.

flowers.name: Mountain Laurel
flowers.wildlife: Provides dense cover for birds. Limited pollinator value.
flowers.description: Spectacular evergreen shrub with clusters of cup-shaped pink and white flowers. One of the most beautiful native flowering shrubs of the eastern mountains. State flower of Connecticut and Pennsylvania.

flowers.name: Cardinal Flower
flowers.wildlife: Primary nectar source for Ruby-throated Hummingbird. Also attracts swallowtail butterflies.
flowers.description: Brilliant scarlet flower spikes along streams and wet meadows. Designed specifically for hummingbird pollination — tubular flowers fit the hummingbird bill perfectly. One of the most hummingbird-attracting native plants in eastern North America.

flowers.name: New England Aster
flowers.wildlife: Critical late-season nectar source for Monarch butterflies migrating south.
flowers.description: Deep purple daisy-like flowers that bloom in late summer and fall when most other flowers have finished. Essential fuel station for Monarch butterflies on their southward migration. Also supports native bees building winter reserves.

flowers.name: Bloodroot
flowers.wildlife: Seeds have elaiosomes — ants carry them underground (myrmecochory).
flowers.description: One of the earliest spring wildflowers — white blooms emerge before the leaves fully open, wrapping themselves in a single large leaf. Brilliant orange-red sap inside the root (gives its name) was used as dye by Native Americans. Ephemeral — disappears by summer.

flowers.name: Painted Trillium
flowers.wildlife: Ant-dispersed seeds. Rare and striking wildflower.
flowers.description: The most striking of New Hampshire's native trilliums — white petals with a brilliant crimson V-shaped marking at the base. Found in cool, moist, acidic forest on mountain slopes. Takes up to 10 years to bloom from seed. Never pick — removing the leaves kills the plant.

flowers.name: Turtlehead
flowers.wildlife: Exclusive host plant for Baltimore Checkerspot butterfly caterpillars.
flowers.description: White snapdragon-like flowers on upright stems in wet woodland and stream margins. The flower opening resembles a turtle's head — hence the name. The exclusive larval host plant for the striking Baltimore Checkerspot butterfly, making it essential for this species' survival in New Hampshire.

flowers.name: Labrador Tea
flowers.wildlife: Specialist bog plant. Few insects due to toxic compounds.
flowers.description: Evergreen bog shrub with aromatic leaves and clusters of white flowers — a defining plant of New Hampshire's high-elevation bogs and peatlands. The leaves were historically brewed as tea by indigenous peoples and early settlers, though contain compounds toxic in large quantities. Rust-colored woolly undersides of leaves are distinctive.

flowers.name: Hobblebush
flowers.wildlife: Berries eaten by bears, grouse, and many birds.
flowers.description: A stunning native shrub of cool mountain forest understories — flat-topped white flower clusters surrounded by large sterile outer flowers give it a lacecap appearance in spring. Berries progress from red to black and feed wildlife. The name comes from branches that root where they touch the ground, 'hobbling' hikers.

flowers.name: Wild Sarsaparilla
flowers.wildlife: Berries eaten by many bird species. Deer browse the leaves.
flowers.description: Low-growing woodland plant with a single compound leaf and spherical umbels of tiny white flowers close to the ground. The aromatic roots were used as a flavoring — a key ingredient in traditional root beer. Common in New Hampshire's mixed forest understory, often forming large colonies by underground rhizomes.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Red Clover
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full plant entry for ecological details.
flowers.description: Introduced but naturalized — Vermont's dairy farming heritage reflected in this clover.

flowers.name: Red Columbine
flowers.habitat: Rocky woodland, cliff edges, forest margins
flowers.wildlife: Primary early-season hummingbird flower. Also visited by long-tongued bees.
flowers.description: Nodding red and yellow spurred flowers on delicate stems. The spurs hold nectar accessible only to hummingbirds and long-tongued bees. Self-seeds freely, naturalizing in rocky woodland edges and cliff crevices. One of the most elegant native wildflowers of Vermont's forests.

flowers.name: Wild Bergamot
flowers.wildlife: Attracts over 20 bee species including native bumblebees. Also attracts butterflies and hummingbirds.
flowers.description: Lavender-pink bee balm with square stems (mint family). A powerhouse pollinator plant — one of the most bee-attractive native plants in the Northeast. Aromatic leaves with oregano-like scent. Very drought-tolerant once established.

flowers.name: Interrupted Fern
flowers.wildlife: Provides important nest material for birds.
flowers.description: A stately woodland fern whose fronds are 'interrupted' mid-stem by the brown spore-bearing pinnae — giving the illusion of missing leaflets. One of Vermont's most characteristic native plants, creating beautiful colonies along woodland streams.

flowers.name: Swamp Milkweed
flowers.wildlife: Essential Monarch butterfly host plant and nectar source. Supports 450+ insects.
flowers.description: Pink milkweed adapted to wet conditions. An essential Monarch butterfly host plant — Monarchs will only lay eggs on milkweed. Also supports 450+ other insect species. More refined than common milkweed, suitable for garden borders near water features.

flowers.name: Joe-Pye Weed
flowers.wildlife: Attracts 18+ butterfly species. Major late-summer pollinator plant.
flowers.description: Tall mauve-purple flower clusters reaching 5–7 feet. A powerhouse late-summer pollinator plant that supports 18+ butterfly species and dozens of native bees. Named for a Native American healer who reportedly used it to treat typhoid fever.

flowers.name: Yellow Clintonia
flowers.wildlife: Berries eaten by thrushes. Boreal forest indicator species.
flowers.description: Pale yellow lily flowers on a tall stem above broad glossy leaves in cool moist forest. The metallic blue-purple berries that follow are striking but poisonous. One of Vermont's most characteristic boreal forest wildflowers — its presence indicates a healthy, undisturbed forest ecosystem.

flowers.name: Round-leaved Sundew
flowers.wildlife: Carnivorous — traps insects with sticky glandular hairs.
flowers.description: Vermont's carnivorous bog plant — spoon-shaped leaves covered with glistening red sticky gland-tipped hairs that trap and digest insects. Supplements the nutrient-poor bog environment. Requires undisturbed acidic sphagnum bog habitat increasingly threatened by drainage and development.

flowers.name: Arrowhead
flowers.wildlife: Tubers eaten by ducks and geese. Important aquatic plant.
flowers.description: Pure white three-petaled flowers on distinctive arrow-shaped leaves emerging from Vermont's ponds and slow rivers. The starchy underground tubers were a critical food source for Native Americans and were called 'wapato.' Attracts waterfowl that feed on the tubers. An ecologically important native aquatic plant.

flowers.name: Wild Columbine
flowers.wildlife: First hummingbird flower of spring. 26 bee species.
flowers.description: Red and yellow spurred flowers nodding from rocky slopes throughout Vermont. One of the most elegant native wildflowers — designed specifically for Ruby-throated Hummingbird pollination, with spurs accessible only to long-tongued pollinators. Self-seeds freely in appropriate rocky, thin-soiled conditions. Essential early-season hummingbird fuel.

flowers.name: Hepatica
flowers.wildlife: Critical early bee plant — first nectar of spring.
flowers.description: One of the very first wildflowers of spring — blue, pink, or white flowers emerging from the leaf litter before the snow has fully retreated, often flowering through snow. The leathery three-lobed leaves that give it its name (liver-leaf) overwinter green. A beloved Vermont spring wildflower that signals the end of winter.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Mayflower (Trailing Arbutus)
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full plant entry for ecological details.
flowers.description: Massachusetts's state flower — one of the first flowers of spring, named for the Pilgrims' ship.

flowers.name: Mayflower (Trailing Arbutus)
flowers.wildlife: Pollinated by queen bumblebees emerging from hibernation.
flowers.description: Massachusetts' state flower — the first flower to bloom each spring in sandy pine forests. Intensely fragrant pink and white flowers hug the ground beneath pine needles. Nearly impossible to transplant — leave it completely alone. Its appearance heralded spring for the Pilgrims who arrived on the Mayflower.

flowers.name: Blue Wild Indigo
flowers.habitat: Open woodland, meadow edges, dry slopes
flowers.wildlife: Host plant for Wild Indigo Duskywing and Clouded Sulphur butterflies.
flowers.description: Deep blue-purple pea-like flowers on an imposing 3–4 foot plant. Extremely long-lived — individual plants live 50+ years once established. Nitrogen-fixing root system improves soil. Striking black seed pods persist through winter.

flowers.name: Bee Balm
flowers.wildlife: Essential hummingbird plant. Supports native bees, hawk moths.
flowers.description: Brilliant red ragged flower heads that are irresistible to Ruby-throated Hummingbirds. Spreads by rhizome in moist rich soil. The leaves make the original Oswego Tea, drunk by colonists after the Boston Tea Party as a substitute for British tea.

flowers.name: Sundew
flowers.wildlife: Carnivorous — traps insects with sticky glandular hairs.
flowers.description: Tiny carnivorous bog plant with spoon-shaped leaves covered in glistening sticky red glandular hairs that trap and digest insects. Supplements nutrients lacking in the poor bog soil. Found in the same acidic sphagnum bogs as pitcher plants.

flowers.name: Wild Geranium
flowers.wildlife: Important early-season bee plant. Attracts 29 bee species.
flowers.description: Lavender-pink five-petaled flowers in woodland and meadow edges. One of the most important early-season native bees plants in the Northeast, attracting 29 recorded bee species. Very adaptable — tolerates both sun and shade. Excellent native garden plant.

flowers.name: Rhodora
flowers.wildlife: Attracts native bumblebee queens emerging from hibernation.
flowers.description: Brilliant purple-pink rhododendron flowers that appear before the leaves in early spring — one of the most beautiful native shrubs of Massachusetts's coastal plain bogs and peaty barrens. Inspired Ralph Waldo Emerson's famous poem 'Rhodora.' Found in the same acidic, moist, nutrient-poor habitats as blueberries and Labrador tea.

flowers.name: Swamp Azalea
flowers.wildlife: Attracts native bees and moths. Fragrant native azalea.
flowers.description: Intensely fragrant white azalea flowering in midsummer along swampy woodland edges and pond margins across Massachusetts. The 'viscosum' (sticky) name refers to the sticky glandular hairs on the flowers. The fragrance is strongest at dusk, attracting sphinx moths as nighttime pollinators.

flowers.name: Closed Gentian
flowers.habitat: Moist meadows, stream banks, woodland edges
flowers.wildlife: Pollinated exclusively by bumblebees strong enough to force open the petals.
flowers.description: Deep blue-violet bottle-shaped flowers that never fully open — pollinated exclusively by bumblebees powerful enough to force their way inside. One of the most striking late-season wildflowers of Massachusetts meadows and stream banks. A true autumn flower blooming into October.

flowers.name: Steeplebush
flowers.habitat: Wet meadows, pond margins, bog edges
flowers.wildlife: Native bees and butterflies. Common wetland shrub.
flowers.description: Rosy-pink cone-shaped flower spikes rising above woolly-white-backed leaves in wet meadows across Massachusetts. One of the most ornamental native shrubs for moist conditions. The woolly white undersides of the leaves make it identifiable even when not in flower. A defining plant of New England wetland meadows.

flowers.name: Fringed Orchid
flowers.wildlife: Pollinated by sphinx moths — night pollinator.
flowers.description: A stunning native orchid of moist meadows and wet woodland edges across Massachusetts — tall spikes of intensely fragrant lavender-purple fringed flowers. Pollinated by sphinx moths (hummingbird moths) attracted by the nighttime fragrance. One of the largest and most spectacular native orchids of New England. Never pick or transplant.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Violet
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full plant entry for ecological details.
flowers.description: Rhode Island's state flower — the common blue violet, host to all Fritillary butterflies.

flowers.name: Violet (Common Blue)
flowers.wildlife: Host plant for all Fritillary butterfly species. Essential butterfly plant.
flowers.description: Rhode Island's state flower — the common blue violet found in lawns, woodland edges, and disturbed ground. Despite being treated as a weed, it is the sole host plant for all Fritillary butterfly caterpillars. Edible flowers used in salads and as garnish.

flowers.name: Seaside Goldenrod
flowers.wildlife: Supports 115+ bee species. Critical late-season coastal pollinator plant.
flowers.description: Salt-tolerant goldenrod found along Rhode Island's entire coastline — dunes, salt marshes, and beach margins. One of the most ecologically important coastal plants, supporting 115+ bee species as a critical late-season nectar source when most plants have finished.

flowers.name: Swamp Rose
flowers.wildlife: Dense thorny thickets provide bird nesting habitat. Hips eaten by 50+ bird species.
flowers.description: Native rose of wetland margins and stream banks — not a garden rose but a true wild native. Single pink flowers mature into red hips that feed over 50 bird species through winter. Dense thorny thickets provide critical nesting habitat.

flowers.name: Butterfly Weed
flowers.wildlife: Essential Monarch host plant. Most insect-attracting native plant in North America by some measures.
flowers.description: Brilliant orange milkweed — the most insect-attractive native plant in North America by some research. Essential Monarch butterfly host plant. Unlike other milkweeds, prefers dry sandy soil. No milky sap. Extremely drought-tolerant once established — taproot goes 18+ inches deep.

flowers.name: Blue-Eyed Grass
flowers.wildlife: Attracts native bees. Low-growing meadow plant.
flowers.description: Despite its name, a member of the iris family — not a grass. Delicate blue-violet six-petaled flowers with yellow centers on grass-like stems. Found in moist meadows and grassy areas throughout Rhode Island. Charming and often overlooked.

flowers.name: Pasture Rose
flowers.habitat: Dry open woodland, roadsides, rocky slopes
flowers.wildlife: Hips eaten by over 20 bird species. Nesting cover.
flowers.description: Rhode Island's most widespread native rose — single pink five-petaled flowers on a low-growing shrub of dry, rocky, open habitats. The bright red rose hips that follow provide critical winter food for birds including ruffed grouse, catbirds, and robins. Far more ecologically valuable than introduced ornamental roses.

flowers.name: Steeplebush
flowers.wildlife: Attracts native bees and small butterflies.
flowers.description: Cone-shaped deep pink flower spikes on woolly-stemmed shrubs in Rhode Island's wet meadows and along stream banks. The woolly white undersides of the leaves are distinctive. One of the most ornamental native shrubs for wet, sunny conditions. Blooms when most shrubs have finished.

flowers.name: Sundew
flowers.habitat: Sphagnum bogs — rare in Rhode Island
flowers.wildlife: Carnivorous. Important indicator of bog ecosystem health.
flowers.description: Rhode Island's rare carnivorous bog plant — found only in a few remaining sphagnum bogs in the state. The glistening sticky gland-tipped hairs trap and digest insects to supplement nutrients from the nutrient-poor bog water. An indicator of pristine, undisturbed bog habitat — its presence signals a healthy ecosystem.

flowers.name: Wild Lupine
flowers.wildlife: Sole host plant for Karner Blue butterfly. Nitrogen fixer.
flowers.description: Tall purple-blue flower spikes in Rhode Island's sandy barrens and dry open areas. The sole larval host plant for the federally endangered Karner Blue butterfly — without wild lupine this butterfly cannot survive. Rhode Island's remaining sandy coastal plain habitats are critical for this species. Nitrogen-fixing roots improve poor sandy soil.

flowers.name: Swamp Candles (Yellow Loosestrife)
flowers.habitat: Wetland margins, pond shores, wet meadows
flowers.wildlife: Specialist oil-collecting native bees. Wetland indicator.
flowers.description: Brilliant yellow flower spikes in Rhode Island's freshwater wetlands and pond margins. Often overlooked because it shares the common name 'loosestrife' with the invasive purple loosestrife — but this is a native with important ecological value. Specialist native bees in the genus Macropis collect floral oils from its petals to line their nest cells.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Mountain Laurel
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full plant entry for ecological details.
flowers.description: Connecticut's state flower — spectacular native shrub with intricate flowers.

flowers.name: Mountain Laurel
flowers.wildlife: Dense cover for nesting birds. Limited but specialist pollinator value.
flowers.description: Connecticut's state flower and one of the most spectacular native flowering shrubs in eastern North America. Intricate cup-shaped pink and white flowers with a unique catapult mechanism that flings pollen onto visiting bees. Poisonous — all parts toxic to humans and animals.

flowers.name: Bloodroot
flowers.wildlife: Ant-dispersed seeds. Spring ephemeral.
flowers.description: One of the earliest spring wildflowers in Connecticut's deciduous forests. A single large leaf wraps the white flower until it opens. Brilliant orange-red sap was used as a dye and insect repellent by Native Americans. Disappears completely by midsummer — a true spring ephemeral.

flowers.name: Nodding Onion
flowers.habitat: Rocky outcrops, open woodland, dry slopes
flowers.wildlife: Attracts native bees and beetles. Edible native.
flowers.description: Graceful native allium with delicate pink to white flower clusters that nod downward at the tip. All parts edible — used like chives or green onions by Native Americans. Grows from rocky outcrops and dry slopes where few other plants thrive.

flowers.name: Spotted Touch-Me-Not (Jewelweed)
flowers.habitat: Wet woodland, stream banks, shaded seeps
flowers.wildlife: Essential hummingbird plant. Also attracts sphinx moths and native bees.
flowers.description: Bright orange spotted flowers on succulent stems along shaded stream banks. Seeds in ripe pods explode when touched — giving the 'touch-me-not' name and dispersing seeds. The juice from crushed stems is a folk remedy for poison ivy rash — remarkably often found growing near it.

flowers.name: Wild Columbine
flowers.habitat: Rocky woodland, cliff faces, dry slopes
flowers.wildlife: First hummingbird flower of spring in Connecticut.
flowers.description: Red and yellow spurred flowers of rocky woodlands and cliff faces. The first hummingbird nectar flower to bloom each spring — critical fuel for Ruby-throated Hummingbirds arriving from Central America. Self-seeds freely in appropriate conditions.

flowers.name: Turk's Cap Lily
flowers.wildlife: Essential hummingbird plant. Swallowtail butterflies.
flowers.description: Connecticut's most dramatic native lily — tall stems reaching 6–8 feet with swept-back orange-red spotted petals forming the 'turk's cap' shape. Once common in Connecticut's moist meadows, now much reduced by habitat loss and deer browsing. The largest native lily in North America and one of the most spectacular wildflowers of the Northeast.

flowers.name: Fringed Loosestrife
flowers.wildlife: Specialist oil-collecting native bees (Macropis).
flowers.description: Nodding yellow flowers on a graceful native loosestrife of Connecticut's moist woodland and stream edges. Unlike the invasive purple loosestrife, this native provides excellent ecological value — specialist native bees (Macropis species) collect floral oils from its petals to line their nest cells.

flowers.name: Blue Cohosh
flowers.wildlife: Berries attract birds. Important woodland herb.
flowers.description: Small purple-blue flowers emerge with the distinctive blue-green foliage in Connecticut's rich deciduous woodland. The metallic-blue toxic berries that follow attract birds for seed dispersal. A significant medicinal plant of eastern woodland — used by Native Americans for childbirth and fever. Increasingly uncommon due to forest understory deer pressure.

flowers.name: Pink Lady's Slipper
flowers.wildlife: Bumblebee specialist. Deceptive pollination.
flowers.description: Connecticut's most celebrated native orchid — a stunning pink slipper-shaped flower that grows in the acidic soil under pines and oaks. Has a specific mycorrhizal fungus relationship — never transplant or pick. Takes 10–17 years to bloom from seed. Pollinators enter the slipper and must push past the stamens to exit, ensuring pollination without offering nectar as a reward.

flowers.name: Cardinal Flower
flowers.habitat: Stream banks, wet meadows, woodland edges
flowers.wildlife: Primary hummingbird plant. Essential for Ruby-throated Hummingbird.
flowers.description: Brilliant scarlet flower spikes along Connecticut's streams and wet meadows — one of the most hummingbird-attractive native plants in eastern North America. The tubular flowers are the perfect size for a hummingbird bill and are inaccessible to most bees. A must-have for any Connecticut garden aiming to attract hummingbirds.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Rose
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full plant entry for ecological details.
flowers.description: New York's state flower — the rose, reflecting the state's cultural diversity.

flowers.name: Rose Pogonia
flowers.wildlife: Pollinated by native bumblebees — deceptive (no nectar).
flowers.description: A native orchid of bogs and wet meadows — one of New York's most beautiful native orchids. Single rose-pink flower with a fringed lip. Found in acidic sphagnum bogs and wet meadows, often growing alongside pitcher plants. Never pick or attempt to transplant — fully protected.

flowers.name: Wild Bergamot
flowers.wildlife: Attracts over 20 native bee species. Essential for native bee diversity.
flowers.description: Lavender-pink bee balm that thrives in dry, sunny conditions across New York. More drought-tolerant than red bee balm (M. didyma). Aromatic leaves with oregano-like scent. One of the most powerful native plants for supporting bee diversity.

flowers.name: Dutchman's Breeches
flowers.wildlife: Pollinated only by long-tongued bumblebee queens.
flowers.description: Extraordinary white flowers that resemble tiny pantaloons hanging upside down on an arching stem. A spring ephemeral of rich woodland floors — blooms, sets seed, and disappears before the forest canopy leafs out. Pollinated exclusively by queen bumblebees with tongues long enough to reach the nectar in the spurs.

flowers.name: Goldenrod
flowers.wildlife: Supports 115+ bee species, 100+ moth/butterfly species. Most insect-supportive native.
flowers.description: Often blamed for hay fever (it's the wind-pollinated ragweed that causes allergies — goldenrod pollen is too heavy for wind). Actually one of the most ecologically important native plants in the Northeast — supports 115+ bee species, 100+ moth and butterfly species, and feeds countless birds through the seeds.

flowers.name: Trout Lily
flowers.wildlife: Ant-dispersed seeds. Spring ephemeral — disappears by June.
flowers.description: Yellow nodding lily with beautifully mottled brown-and-green leaves resembling brook trout. Spreads slowly through underground stolons to form large colonies that can be hundreds of years old. A true spring ephemeral — leaves and flowers both disappear by June. Takes 7 years to first bloom from seed.

flowers.name: Wild Lupine
flowers.wildlife: Sole host plant for the endangered Karner Blue butterfly. Nitrogen fixer.
flowers.description: Tall spikes of blue-purple pea flowers in New York's sandy pine barrens and dry open areas. The sole larval host plant for the federally endangered Karner Blue butterfly — without wild lupine, this butterfly cannot survive. New York's pine barrens hold critical populations. Nitrogen-fixing roots improve poor sandy soil.

flowers.name: Jack-in-the-Pulpit
flowers.wildlife: Berries eaten by wood thrush. Unusual flower structure.
flowers.description: One of New York's most architecturally interesting wildflowers — a spathe (the 'pulpit') curving over the spadix ('Jack'). Separate male and female plants that can switch sex depending on energy reserves — a remarkable adaptation. Brilliant red berries replace the flowers in fall. Calcium oxalate crystals in all parts cause intense burning if eaten raw.

flowers.name: Bloodroot
flowers.wildlife: Ant-dispersed seeds. Spring ephemeral.
flowers.description: One of New York's earliest spring wildflowers — pure white flowers with golden stamens emerging from the forest floor before the trees leaf out. A single large leaf wraps the bud until it opens. Brilliant orange-red sap in the root was used as face paint and fabric dye by the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) people. Disappears entirely by early summer.

flowers.name: Bottle Gentian
flowers.habitat: Moist meadows, woodland edges, stream banks
flowers.wildlife: Bumblebee specialist — only bees strong enough to open the petals can pollinate.
flowers.description: Deep blue-violet closed flowers that never fully open — pollinated exclusively by bumblebees strong enough to force their way inside and out. One of the most striking late-season wildflowers of New York's moist meadows. A true autumn flower that continues blooming into October when most plants have finished. Indicates a healthy, undisturbed meadow ecosystem.

flowers.name: Pasque Flower
flowers.habitat: Rocky prairies, limestone outcrops — rare in NY
flowers.wildlife: Early bee plant. Spring ephemeral.
flowers.description: One of the earliest prairie wildflowers — purple to lavender silky-haired flowers emerging in early spring before the leaves fully unfold. Found in New York's rare calcareous grassland and limestone outcrop habitats in western counties. A plant of open, well-drained, slightly alkaline soils. Feathery seed heads persist through summer.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Common Blue Violet
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full plant entry for ecological details.
flowers.description: New Jersey's state flower — the common blue violet found throughout the state.

flowers.name: Swamp Pink
flowers.habitat: Atlantic coastal plain seeps and bogs
flowers.wildlife: Rare and federally threatened. Pollinated by early spring bees.
flowers.description: One of New Jersey's rarest native wildflowers — federally threatened. Striking pink flower spike rising from a rosette of evergreen leaves in freshwater seeps and bogs of the Atlantic coastal plain. New Jersey has the largest remaining populations. Never disturb.

flowers.name: Turkeybeard
flowers.wildlife: Attracts native bees. New Jersey Pine Barrens specialist.
flowers.description: A dramatic wildflower of New Jersey's Pine Barrens — long grass-like leaves topped with a dense spike of tiny white flowers. Found almost exclusively in the unique acidic sandy soils of the Pine Barrens ecosystem. Requires fire-adapted habitat to thrive.

flowers.name: Butterfly Weed
flowers.wildlife: Essential Monarch host plant. Extremely insect-rich.
flowers.description: Brilliant orange milkweed — one of the most beautiful and ecologically important native wildflowers of New Jersey's dry sandy habitats. Essential host plant for Monarch butterflies. The deep taproot makes it drought-resistant but impossible to transplant successfully.

flowers.name: Lizard's Tail
flowers.wildlife: Provides aquatic habitat structure. Attracts bees.
flowers.description: Fragrant white flower spikes that curve at the tip like a lizard's tail. Forms dense colonies in shallow freshwater wetlands and along stream margins. One of the few native plants that can grow in standing water. Heart-shaped leaves remain attractive all season.

flowers.name: Wild Pink
flowers.wildlife: Attracts sphinx moths (night pollination) and native bees.
flowers.description: Brilliant hot pink flowers on rocky outcrops and dry sandy woodland edges. One of New Jersey's most colorful spring wildflowers. Sticky stem and leaf glands (the 'catch-fly' trait) trap small insects — possibly to prevent them from stealing nectar without pollinating.

flowers.name: Bald Cypress
flowers.habitat: Freshwater swamps, stream banks — at northern range edge
flowers.wildlife: Critical wildlife habitat. Cavity nesting birds. Fish habitat.
flowers.description: The famous 'swamp tree' reaches its northern range limit in New Jersey's coastal plain swamps. Unusual deciduous conifer with feathery foliage and distinctive 'knees' (pneumatophores) that help the roots breathe in waterlogged soil. Ancient trees provide critical cavity-nesting habitat for wood ducks and other wildlife.

flowers.name: Wild Columbine
flowers.habitat: Rocky slopes, cedar glades, cliff faces
flowers.wildlife: First hummingbird flower of spring. 26 bee species recorded.
flowers.description: Red and yellow spurred flowers nodding from rocky slopes and cliff faces throughout New Jersey. The first flower Ruby-throated Hummingbirds visit upon returning from Central America each spring — critical fuel for northward migration. Grows naturally from rock crevices in thin, poor soil where little else survives. Self-seeds readily once established.

flowers.name: Grass Pink Orchid
flowers.habitat: Acidic bogs, wet meadows — Pine Barrens specialist
flowers.wildlife: Pollinated by bumblebees — deceptive (no nectar offered).
flowers.description: A stunning native orchid of New Jersey's Pine Barrens bogs and acidic wet meadows — bright pink flowers with a distinctive yellow-tipped lip at the top (inverted from most orchids). Pollinates bumblebees deceptively — they land on the flower lip expecting pollen but instead pollinate the flower while trying to right themselves. One of New Jersey's most beautiful Pine Barrens natives.

flowers.name: Rose Pogonia
flowers.wildlife: Native bumblebee specialist. Bog indicator species.
flowers.description: A delicate native orchid of New Jersey's sphagnum bogs and acidic wet meadows — a single rose-pink flower on a slender stem, delicately fragrant. Found in the same bog ecosystem as pitcher plants, sundews, and cranberries. Requires undisturbed acidic, nutrient-poor wetland habitat. Never pick — each flower represents years of slow growth.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Mountain Laurel
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full plant entry for ecological details.
flowers.description: Pennsylvania's state flower — shared with Connecticut, this spectacular native shrub.

flowers.name: Mountain Laurel
flowers.wildlife: State flower. Specialist bee habitat. Dense bird cover.
flowers.description: Pennsylvania's state flower — spectacular native shrub with intricate pink and white flowers. The unique catapult stamen mechanism flings pollen onto visiting bumblebees. All parts poisonous — toxic honey was historically produced from its nectar. One of the defining plants of the Appalachian mountain landscape.

flowers.name: Wild Senna
flowers.habitat: Moist meadows, stream banks, open woodland
flowers.wildlife: Host plant for Cloudless Sulphur and other sulphur butterflies.
flowers.description: Tall yellow-flowered native legume of moist meadows and stream banks. A powerhouse pollinator plant that hosts multiple sulphur butterfly species. Nitrogen-fixing roots improve soil. Seeds were historically used as a coffee substitute.

flowers.name: Blue Cohosh
flowers.wildlife: Seeds attract birds — blue berries despite being toxic.
flowers.description: Small purplish-blue flowers on bluish-green foliage in rich woodland. The striking metallic-blue berries that follow are toxic but attract birds. Long used medicinally by Native Americans for childbirth — contains compounds that stimulate uterine contractions. A significant woodland herb of Pennsylvania's forests.

flowers.name: Wild Ginger
flowers.wildlife: Pollinated by ground-level insects. Ant-dispersed seeds.
flowers.description: Low ground-covering plant of rich woodland with heart-shaped leaves hiding small brownish-red flowers at soil level — pollinated by beetles and flies that emerge from the leaf litter. The aromatic roots were used as a ginger substitute. Forms dense fragrant ground cover in shade.

flowers.name: Fringed Gentian
flowers.wildlife: Attracts native bees. Late-season rarity.
flowers.description: One of the most beautiful and rarest native wildflowers in Pennsylvania — intensely blue fringed petals that close in clouds and at night, opening only in full sun. Annual or biennial — appears unpredictably. Sensitive to habitat disturbance. A highlight of any fall wildflower walk.

flowers.name: Dutchman's Breeches
flowers.wildlife: Pollinated exclusively by queen bumblebees with long tongues.
flowers.description: Extraordinary white pantaloon-shaped flowers dangling from arching stems in Pennsylvania's rich woodland. A spring ephemeral that blooms, sets seed, and vanishes before the forest canopy closes. Pollinated exclusively by queen bumblebees whose tongues are long enough to reach nectar hidden in the twin spurs. One of the most architecturally unique wildflowers of the Northeast.

flowers.name: Pink Azalea (Pinxterbloom)
flowers.habitat: Dry to moist woodland, rocky slopes
flowers.wildlife: Native bumblebees and sphinx moths.
flowers.description: Pennsylvania's native azalea — fragrant pink flowers appearing before or with the emerging leaves on woodland slopes throughout the state. Far superior to introduced Asian azaleas for native wildlife. The fragrance attracts both bumblebees by day and sphinx moths at dusk. Forms beautiful colonies on rocky slopes in the Ridge and Valley region.

flowers.name: Pokeweed
flowers.wildlife: Berries eaten by 33 bird species. Important wildlife plant despite toxicity.
flowers.description: A dramatic native plant reaching 10 feet — white flower racemes followed by deep purple-black berries on magenta stems that are among the most ornamental of any native plant. Despite the toxicity (all parts toxic to humans and livestock), pokeweed berries are eaten by 33 bird species and are critical wildlife food. The berries produce a brilliant purple-red dye historically used by Native Americans and colonists.

flowers.name: Spicebush
flowers.wildlife: Host plant for Spicebush Swallowtail. Critical early nectar.
flowers.description: One of Pennsylvania's most ecologically important native shrubs — tiny yellow flowers appear in early spring before any other native shrub, providing critical first nectar for queen bumblebees emerging from hibernation. Host plant for the Spicebush Swallowtail butterfly, one of Pennsylvania's most beautiful. The berries turn brilliant red in fall and are devoured by migrating birds.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Peach Blossom
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full plant entry for ecological details.
flowers.description: Delaware's state flower — honoring its agricultural heritage as a peach-growing state.

flowers.name: Peach Blossom (Represented by Peach)
flowers.habitat: Orchards, open areas — state flower but not native wildflower
flowers.wildlife: Important early bee food. Not native but deeply embedded in Delaware culture.
flowers.description: Delaware's state flower reflects its agricultural peach-growing heritage rather than a native wildflower. The pink peach blossoms signal spring across Delaware's orchards. Delaware was once the leading peach-producing state before a blight wiped out the industry in the 1890s.

flowers.name: Cardinal Flower
flowers.wildlife: Primary hummingbird plant of Delaware's coastal plain.
flowers.description: Brilliant red flower spikes along Delaware's streams and wetland edges. The tubular flowers are designed specifically for Ruby-throated Hummingbird pollination — the bird's beak brushes the anthers depositing and receiving pollen while hovering. One of the most hummingbird-attractive plants in the eastern US.

flowers.name: Spatterdock
flowers.wildlife: Provides aquatic habitat. Waterfowl eat seeds and rhizomes.
flowers.description: Yellow floating-leaved aquatic plant of Delaware's tidal freshwater rivers and ponds. Large round floating leaves provide shade that cools water for fish. The globular yellow flowers have an unusual brandy-like scent. Waterfowl rely on the seeds and rhizomes for food.

flowers.name: Swamp Azalea
flowers.wildlife: Attracts native bees and butterflies. Fragrant native azalea.
flowers.description: Intensely fragrant white azalea of swampy woodland and wetland edges. The sticky (viscous) flowers release fragrance especially at dusk, attracting moths as well as bees. One of the few native azaleas that thrives in wet conditions.

flowers.name: Golden Club
flowers.habitat: Shallow water, pond edges, tidal wetlands
flowers.wildlife: Aquatic habitat structure. Seeds eaten by waterfowl.
flowers.description: Striking aquatic plant with white spathe and brilliant golden-yellow spadix rising from pond edges and tidal freshwater wetlands in Delaware's coastal plain. The waxy leaves bead water like mercury — hence the folk name 'never wet.' One of the most beautiful native aquatic plants. Seeds and roots were used as food by Native Americans after extensive preparation to remove toxic calcium oxalate crystals.

flowers.name: Marsh Marigold
flowers.habitat: Wet woodland, swamp edges, stream banks
flowers.wildlife: Important early-season bee plant. First nectar of spring.
flowers.description: Brilliant yellow buttercup-like flowers carpeting wet woodland and stream margins in early spring — one of the first wildflowers to bloom in Delaware's wetlands. The sheer number of flowers provides a critical mass of early nectar for queen bumblebees emerging from hibernation. Also called cowslip. All parts toxic when raw — young leaves were boiled as a pot herb historically.

flowers.name: Rose Mallow
flowers.wildlife: Specialist native bees evolved specifically for this genus.
flowers.description: Enormous native hibiscus with plate-sized pink to white flowers rising from Delaware's tidal marshes and freshwater wetland edges. Among the largest flowers of any native plant in the eastern US. Specialist native bees in the genus Ptilothrix and Cemolobus evolved specifically to collect pollen from native Hibiscus — dependent on this plant for survival.

flowers.name: Swamp Milkweed
flowers.habitat: Freshwater wetlands, pond margins, stream banks
flowers.wildlife: Essential Monarch butterfly host plant. Supports 450+ insects.
flowers.description: Pink milkweed of Delaware's freshwater wetlands and pond margins — an essential Monarch butterfly host plant. Unlike common milkweed, this species thrives in wet conditions and has a more refined appearance suitable for garden borders near water features. Also supports 450+ other insect species. One of the most ecologically important native plants for Delaware's wetland habitats.

flowers.name: Blue Wild Indigo
flowers.habitat: Open woodland, meadow edges, stream banks
flowers.wildlife: Host plant for multiple butterfly species. Long-lived perennial.
flowers.description: Deep blue-purple pea-like flowers on an imposing 3–4 foot plant found in Delaware's open woodland and meadow edges. Extremely long-lived — individual plants live 50+ years once established. Nitrogen-fixing root system improves soil. Black seed pods rattle in the wind through winter, providing structural interest in the landscape.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Black-Eyed Susan
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full plant entry for ecological details.
flowers.description: Maryland's state flower — also the flower draped over Preakness Stakes winners.

flowers.name: Black-Eyed Susan
flowers.wildlife: Goldfinches eat seeds. Supports native bees and butterflies.
flowers.description: Maryland's state flower — golden yellow daisies with dark brown centers blanketing roadsides and meadows across the state. Named for the Preakness Stakes winner where they are draped over winning horses. Extremely adaptable and long-blooming — one of the easiest native wildflowers to grow.

flowers.name: Wild Columbine
flowers.habitat: Rocky woodland, cliff edges, shaded slopes
flowers.wildlife: Critical early hummingbird flower. 26 bee species recorded visiting.
flowers.description: Red and yellow spurred flowers of rocky woodland and cliff faces. The first hummingbird flower of spring in Maryland — critical fuel for northward-migrating Ruby-throated Hummingbirds. Self-seeds in appropriate rocky, partly-shaded conditions forming beautiful naturalized colonies.

flowers.name: Wild Blue Phlox
flowers.wildlife: Attracts sphinx moths and swallowtail butterflies. Fragrant.
flowers.description: Fragrant pale lavender-blue flowers carpet the floor of rich deciduous woodland in April and May. One of the most beautiful spring wildflowers of Maryland's forest understory. The fragrance attracts sphinx moths (hummingbird moths) and swallowtail butterflies.

flowers.name: Turk's Cap Lily
flowers.habitat: Moist meadows, woodland edges, stream banks
flowers.wildlife: Essential hummingbird plant. Attracts swallowtail butterflies.
flowers.description: One of the tallest and most dramatic native wildflowers — orange-red reflexed (swept back) petals with heavy spotting on stems reaching 6–8 feet. A stunning accent plant for moist meadow gardens. The largest native lily in North America.

flowers.name: Spicebush
flowers.wildlife: Host plant for Spicebush Swallowtail butterfly. Berries eaten by migrating birds.
flowers.description: One of Maryland's most ecologically important native shrubs — tiny yellow flowers appear before leaves in early spring, providing critical early nectar. Host plant for the stunning Spicebush Swallowtail butterfly. Aromatic leaves, bark, and berries historically used as a spice.

flowers.name: Dutchman's Breeches
flowers.wildlife: Queen bumblebee specialist. Spring ephemeral.
flowers.description: White pantaloon-shaped flowers on arching stems in Maryland's rich woodland ravines. One of the most charming spring ephemerals — blooms, sets seed, and disappears entirely before summer. Found in particularly fine stands along the stream banks of western Maryland's mountain counties. Pollinated exclusively by long-tongued bumblebee queens.

flowers.name: Mayapple
flowers.wildlife: Yellow fruit eaten by box turtles and opossums. Colony-forming.
flowers.description: Large umbrella-like leaves emerge in dense colonies across Maryland's woodland floors, hiding a single waxy white flower underneath. Only the forked (two-leaved) plants produce flowers and edible yellow fruit. The colony may be genetically a single individual spreading by rhizomes — some Maryland colonies are estimated to be centuries old. All parts except ripe fruit are highly toxic.

flowers.name: Columbine
flowers.habitat: Rocky woodland, cliff edges, cedar glades
flowers.wildlife: Critical hummingbird flower. 26 bee species recorded.
flowers.description: Red and yellow spurred flowers of Maryland's rocky woodland and cliff faces — the first hummingbird flower of spring. Critical fuel for Ruby-throated Hummingbirds arriving from Central America. Self-seeds freely in rocky, thin-soiled conditions, forming beautiful naturalized colonies. One of the most elegant native wildflowers of the Shenandoah Valley and Blue Ridge foothills.

flowers.name: Sensitive Fern
flowers.wildlife: Important habitat structure for wetland invertebrates.
flowers.description: A robust native fern of Maryland's wetlands and moist woodland — strongly dimorphic with separate sterile fronds (the 'leaves') and fertile fronds bearing bead-like spore cases that persist through winter. One of the most drought-sensitive native ferns — wilts dramatically in heat, leading to its common name. Forms extensive colonies in wet ground.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: American Dogwood
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full plant entry for ecological details.
flowers.description: Virginia's state flower and tree — the iconic spring-blooming dogwood of eastern woodlands.

flowers.name: American Dogwood
flowers.wildlife: Berries eaten by 36+ bird species. Host to 117 moth/butterfly species.
flowers.description: Virginia's state flower and tree — the iconic white-bracted dogwood that illuminates woodland edges each spring before leaves emerge. The white 'petals' are actually bracts (modified leaves) surrounding the tiny true flowers. Among the most ecologically important understory trees in eastern forests — supports 117 moth and butterfly species and 36+ bird species.

flowers.name: Virginia Bluebells
flowers.wildlife: Important for native bumblebee queens emerging from hibernation. Spring ephemeral.
flowers.description: Among the most beautiful spring wildflowers of Virginia's floodplain forests — masses of nodding sky-blue tubular flowers with pink buds, creating breathtaking drifts along stream banks. A true spring ephemeral — completely dormant by early summer. Named for Virginia, where early botanists first documented it.

flowers.name: Fire Pink
flowers.habitat: Rocky woodland, dry slopes, cliff edges
flowers.wildlife: Hummingbird specialist flower. Bright red signals hummingbird vision.
flowers.description: Brilliant scarlet star-shaped flowers of rocky Virginia woodland and cliff faces. The deep red color and tubular shape are specifically adapted to attract Ruby-throated Hummingbirds — the red color is visible to hummingbirds but less attractive to most insects. One of Virginia's most striking native wildflowers.

flowers.name: Mayapple
flowers.wildlife: Fruit eaten by box turtles and opossums. Seeds dispersed by wildlife.
flowers.description: Large umbrella-like leaves hide a single waxy white flower underneath. Only plants with two leaves (forked stems) produce flowers and fruit. The yellow apple-like fruit is edible when fully ripe but all other parts are highly toxic. Forms extensive colonies in rich woodland — a single colony may be hundreds of years old.

flowers.name: Wild Azalea (Pinxterbloom)
flowers.wildlife: Important native bee plant. Attracts sphinx moths.
flowers.description: Virginia's native azalea — fragrant pink flowers appear before or with the emerging leaves on dry to moist woodland slopes. One of the earliest flowering native shrubs. Often mistaken for the introduced Japanese azaleas — the native version is more fragrant and ecologically valuable.

flowers.name: Trout Lily
flowers.wildlife: Spring ephemeral. Ant-dispersed seeds.
flowers.description: Mottled brown-and-green leaves resembling brook trout emerge in spectacular colonies in Virginia's floodplain forests and rich woodland. Only a tiny fraction of plants bloom — most are non-flowering 'grass-stage' plants connected by underground stolons. A single colony covering an acre may be hundreds of years old. Among the earliest spring wildflowers.

flowers.name: Wild Columbine
flowers.habitat: Rocky woodland, cliff edges, cedar glades
flowers.wildlife: Critical hummingbird flower. 26 bee species recorded.
flowers.description: Red and yellow spurred flowers of Virginia's rocky woodland and cliff faces. Nodding flowers designed specifically for Ruby-throated Hummingbird pollination — the spurs hold nectar accessible only to hummingbirds and long-tongued bees. Self-seeds freely in rocky, thin-soiled conditions. One of the most beautiful native wildflowers of the Shenandoah Valley.

flowers.name: Spicebush
flowers.wildlife: Host plant for Spicebush Swallowtail butterfly. Berries for migrating birds.
flowers.description: One of Virginia's most ecologically important native shrubs — tiny yellow flowers appear in early spring before any other native shrub, providing critical early nectar. The Spicebush Swallowtail butterfly — one of Virginia's most beautiful natives — depends entirely on spicebush and sassafras as larval host plants. Aromatic spicy fragrance in all parts.

flowers.name: Wild Blue Phlox
flowers.wildlife: Attracts sphinx moths and swallowtail butterflies. Fragrant.
flowers.description: Clouds of fragrant pale lavender-blue flowers carpeting Virginia's rich deciduous woodland floors in spring — one of the most beautiful spring wildflowers for the shaded garden. Adaptable to both sun and shade. The fragrance is particularly strong at dusk, attracting sphinx moths as nighttime pollinators alongside swallowtail butterflies by day.

flowers.name: Wild Ginger
flowers.wildlife: Ground beetle pollinated. Ant-dispersed seeds.
flowers.description: Heart-shaped aromatic leaves forming dense ground cover in Virginia's rich woodland, hiding small brownish-red flowers at soil level. Pollinated by beetles and flies emerging from the leaf litter. The roots have an authentic ginger aroma and were used as a spice substitute by both Native Americans and early settlers. Forms fragrant, beautiful colonies in shaded conditions.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Rhododendron
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full plant entry for ecological details.
flowers.description: West Virginia's state flower — spectacular mountain shrub defining Appalachian landscapes.

flowers.name: Rhododendron
flowers.habitat: Mountain slopes, stream banks, cool ravines
flowers.wildlife: Dense thickets provide critical bird nesting habitat in mountain areas.
flowers.description: West Virginia's state flower — the Rosebay Rhododendron that forms spectacular dense thickets on mountain slopes and cool ravines. One of the defining plants of Appalachian mountain landscapes. Massive clusters of pale pink flowers. All parts toxic — produces a toxic honey called 'mad honey' in areas with dense populations.

flowers.name: Trillium (Great White)
flowers.wildlife: Ant-dispersed seeds. Slow-growing forest wildflower.
flowers.description: The largest and most spectacular native trillium — pure white three-petaled flowers aging to pink. West Virginia's mountain forests host substantial populations. Takes 7–10 years to bloom from seed. Never pick or transplant — picking removes the only leaf structure, eventually killing the plant. Overharvested in much of its range.

flowers.name: Flame Azalea
flowers.habitat: Mountain ridges, dry slopes — Appalachian specialist
flowers.wildlife: Attracts bumblebees, sphinx moths, hummingbirds.
flowers.description: One of the most spectacular native plants in North America — brilliant orange to flame-red flowers on mountain ridges of the Appalachians. William Bartram called it 'the most gay and brilliant flowering shrub yet known' in 1791. West Virginia's mountain ridges host some of the finest displays anywhere.

flowers.name: Wild Bergamot
flowers.wildlife: Over 20 native bee species. Hummingbirds.
flowers.description: Lavender bee balm of dry mountain meadows throughout West Virginia's hills. Aromatic minty-oregano fragrance. An exceptionally important plant for native bee diversity — recorded hosting over 20 bee species. More drought-tolerant than red bee balm.

flowers.name: Bloodroot
flowers.wildlife: Ant-dispersed seeds. Spring ephemeral.
flowers.description: One of West Virginia's first spring wildflowers — pure white blooms emerging from the forest floor before the trees leaf out, each wrapped in a single large leaf. The brilliant orange-red sap in the root was used as face paint by Native Americans. Disappears entirely by midsummer. Found in particularly fine stands in the rich cove forests of the Monongahela National Forest.

flowers.name: Dutchman's Breeches
flowers.wildlife: Queen bumblebee specialist. Spring ephemeral.
flowers.description: Pantaloon-shaped white flowers of West Virginia's rich cove forests and rocky slopes. Among the most charming spring ephemerals of the Appalachians — appears, blooms, sets seed, and vanishes in just 6–8 weeks. West Virginia's mixed mesophytic forests contain some of the finest stands of spring ephemerals in the entire Appalachian region.

flowers.name: Ramps (Wild Leek)
flowers.wildlife: Ant-dispersed seeds. Cultural significance to Appalachian communities.
flowers.description: West Virginia's most culturally significant native plant — ramps emerge in early spring in dense colonies in rich woodland, with broad garlic-scented leaves that disappear before the flowers emerge. The subject of annual festivals throughout West Virginia and Appalachia. An important traditional food of both indigenous peoples and Appalachian communities. Harvest sustainably — never take more than 10% of a colony.

flowers.name: Yellow Lady's Slipper
flowers.wildlife: Bumblebee specialist. Native orchid.
flowers.description: West Virginia's native orchid — a beautiful yellow slipper orchid of rich moist woodland and stream banks in the mountains. The inflated yellow pouch traps bees that must push past the stigma and anthers to escape — ensuring pollination. Takes 10+ years to bloom from seed. Never pick or transplant. Found in particularly fine populations in the Monongahela National Forest.

flowers.name: Great Rhododendron
flowers.wildlife: Dense nesting cover for birds. Nectar for bumblebees.
flowers.description: West Virginia's state flower — the Rosebay Rhododendron that forms spectacular dense thickets on mountain slopes and cool ravines, creating the famous 'rhododendron hells' that early settlers found nearly impenetrable. One of the defining plants of Appalachian mountain landscapes. Massive clusters of pale pink flowers. Can live for centuries.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Dogwood
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full plant entry for ecological details.
flowers.description: North Carolina's state flower — shared with Virginia, the beloved spring dogwood.

flowers.name: Carolina Lily
flowers.habitat: Dry woodland, mountain slopes — Appalachian specialist
flowers.wildlife: Hummingbirds and swallowtail butterflies.
flowers.description: North Carolina's endemic native lily — orange-red strongly reflexed petals with heavy maroon spotting. Found from the Piedmont to the mountains. Closely related to Turk's Cap Lily but more drought-tolerant. Named for French botanist André Michaux who explored North Carolina's mountains extensively.

flowers.name: Venus Flytrap
flowers.habitat: NC/SC coastal plain longleaf pine savannas — very restricted
flowers.wildlife: Carnivorous — traps insects. Pollinated by native bees (pollinators not trapped).
flowers.description: North Carolina's most famous native plant — the Venus Flytrap is found naturally only within a 75-mile radius of Wilmington, NC. One of the most remarkable plants on Earth. Critically threatened by habitat loss and collection. Fully protected — collection from the wild is a felony in North Carolina.

flowers.name: Mountain Laurel
flowers.wildlife: Dense cover for Appalachian birds.
flowers.description: Spectacular native shrub with intricate pink and white flowers blanketing North Carolina's mountain slopes in late spring. One of the defining plants of the Southern Appalachian landscape. Rhododendron and mountain laurel together create the famous 'balds' and heath forests of the Blue Ridge.

flowers.name: Trout Lily
flowers.wildlife: Spring ephemeral. Ant-dispersed seeds.
flowers.description: Mottled brown-and-green leaves (resembling brook trout) emerge in dense colonies in North Carolina's rich woodland. Only a small percentage of plants in a colony bloom in any given year. Forms colonies that may be hundreds of years old. Among the first wildflowers of spring.

flowers.name: Pink Muhly Grass
flowers.wildlife: Seeds eaten by ground-feeding birds. Provides habitat structure.
flowers.description: Cloud-like masses of pink-purple seedheads cover rocky outcrops and dry roadsides across the NC Piedmont and coastal plain each fall. One of the most dramatic native plants in autumn landscapes. Increasingly used in native plant gardens for its spectacular fall display.

flowers.name: Oconee Bells
flowers.habitat: Mountain ravines, stream banks — extremely rare
flowers.wildlife: Early bee plant. One of the rarest native wildflowers in the world.
flowers.description: One of the rarest native wildflowers in the world — white bell-shaped flowers with fringed petals in a handful of locations in North Carolina's Blue Ridge mountain ravines. Lost to science for 100 years after Michaux first collected it in 1788 — rediscovered in 1877. Named for the Oconee River region. North Carolina contains the vast majority of wild populations globally. Fully protected.

flowers.name: Atamasco Lily
flowers.wildlife: Attracts native bees. Spring bulb wildflower.
flowers.description: Pure white funnel-shaped lily emerging mysteriously in early spring in wet woodland and roadside ditches across the NC Coastal Plain and Piedmont. Known locally as 'Easter lily' and 'rain lily' — often appearing in great numbers after spring rains. Bulbs are toxic. A stunning native wildflower increasingly appreciated in naturalistic garden settings.

flowers.name: Gray's Lily
flowers.wildlife: Hummingbird plant. Southern Appalachian endemic.
flowers.description: One of North Carolina's rarest native plants — a small red-orange lily found only on the high-elevation grassy balds of the southern Appalachians. Named for botanist Asa Gray. Found in only a handful of locations globally, primarily in western North Carolina. Federally listed as threatened. The high-elevation grassy balds it requires are themselves a rare and poorly understood ecosystem.

flowers.name: Galax
flowers.wildlife: Bees. Important ground cover plant.
flowers.description: An Appalachian endemic — round, leathery, evergreen leaves that turn brilliant bronze-red in fall and winter, with small white flower spikes in summer. Galax leaves are among the most harvested native plants in the Appalachians for the floral industry — sustainably harvested leaves are used in wreaths and arrangements. Forms dense ground-covering colonies in mountain woodland.

flowers.name: Catesby's Trillium
flowers.wildlife: Ant-dispersed seeds. Protected in several states.
flowers.description: A nodding pink trillium of the southern Appalachian mountain woodland — one of North Carolina's most beautiful native wildflowers. Flowers nod downward on a bent stalk, unique among eastern trilliums. Named for Mark Catesby, the first naturalist to document many Carolina plants. Takes 7+ years to bloom from seed. Never pick — protected in several Appalachian states.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Yellow Jessamine
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full plant entry for ecological details.
flowers.description: South Carolina's state flower — fragrant yellow trumpet flowers blooming in late winter.

flowers.name: Yellow Jessamine
flowers.wildlife: Early spring nectar source when little else blooms. Attracts native bees.
flowers.description: South Carolina's state flower — fragrant yellow trumpet flowers that bloom as early as January along fence rows, roadsides, and in open woodland. One of the first flowers of the year in the coastal plain. Despite its beauty, all parts are severely toxic — it has caused deaths when confused with edible wild plants.

flowers.name: Swamp Rose Mallow
flowers.habitat: Freshwater marshes, pond margins, tidal wetlands
flowers.wildlife: Attracts specialist native bees. Important wetland plant.
flowers.description: Enormous native hibiscus with dinner-plate-sized pink to white flowers — among the largest flowers of any native plant in the eastern US. Found in coastal plain freshwater marshes and pond edges. Attracts specialist native bees that evolved specifically to collect its pollen.

flowers.name: Atamasco Lily
flowers.wildlife: Attracts native bees. Spring bulb wildflower.
flowers.description: Pure white funnel-shaped lily that emerges mysteriously from wet woodland floors and floodplains in early spring — sometimes in such abundance it creates white drifts. Also called 'Easter lily of the South.' Bulbs are toxic. A stunning spring wildflower increasingly rare in many areas due to habitat loss.

flowers.name: Pitcher Plant (Parrot)
flowers.habitat: Coastal plain pine savannas, pitcher plant bogs
flowers.wildlife: Carnivorous — traps aquatic invertebrates when flooded. Unique carnivore.
flowers.description: One of South Carolina's most unusual native plants — a carnivorous pitcher plant unique in that it traps aquatic invertebrates when its horizontal pitchers flood, unlike the vertical pitchers of most species. Found in the increasingly rare longleaf pine savanna ecosystem of the coastal plain.

flowers.name: Purple Coneflower
flowers.wildlife: Goldfinches eat seeds through winter. Supports 50+ bee species.
flowers.description: Large pink-purple daisy-like flowers with a prominent spiny orange-brown center cone. One of the most important native plants for pollinators in South Carolina — supports 50+ bee species and provides critical winter food for goldfinches that cling to the seed heads. The medicinal properties of echinacea are well-documented.

flowers.name: Wild Ginger
flowers.wildlife: Ground beetle pollinated. Ant-dispersed seeds.
flowers.description: South Carolina's native wild ginger — different from the northern species, this southeastern specialist has beautifully mottled evergreen leaves and small brown jug-shaped flowers hidden at soil level. The aromatic roots have a true ginger scent. Forms attractive evergreen ground cover in shaded acidic woodland — one of the best native ground covers for the Southeast.

flowers.name: Carolina Jessamine
flowers.wildlife: Important early nectar source. Attracts native bees.
flowers.description: Fragrant yellow trumpet flowers covering woodland edges and fence rows across South Carolina in late winter and early spring. One of the first flowers of the year — critical early nectar when little else blooms. Despite being the state flower, all parts are severely toxic — has caused human deaths. The fragrance is sweet and distinctive.

flowers.name: Sundew (Thread-leaved)
flowers.habitat: Coastal plain savannas — extremely rare globally
flowers.wildlife: Carnivorous — traps insects. Critical bog ecosystem indicator.
flowers.description: Thread-leaved sundew — one of South Carolina's most extraordinary native plants. Long, thin, thread-like leaves covered in glistening red sticky glands that trap insects. Found almost exclusively in the increasingly rare longleaf pine savanna ecosystem of the Atlantic coastal plain. Pink flowers on long stems rise above the carnivorous leaves. One of the world's most geographically restricted sundew species.

flowers.name: Walter's Violet
flowers.wildlife: Host for all Fritillary butterfly species. Early bee plant.
flowers.description: A low-growing native violet of rocky woodland slopes and Carolina sandhills — smaller and earlier blooming than the common blue violet. Like all violets, it is the sole larval host plant for all Fritillary butterfly species. The presence of native violets in a garden directly supports the entire Fritillary butterfly lifecycle.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Cherokee Rose
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full plant entry for ecological details.
flowers.description: Georgia's state flower — introduced from China but deeply woven into Georgia's history.

flowers.name: Cherokee Rose
flowers.habitat: Roadsides, woodland edges — naturalized, not native
flowers.wildlife: Provides dense thorny cover for birds.
flowers.description: Georgia's state flower — though ironically not native to North America. Introduced from China, it naturalized across the South and is deeply associated with Georgia's landscape. Named for the Cherokee people who traded the plant across the Southeast. Single white five-petaled flowers with golden stamens.

flowers.name: Coreopsis (Threadleaf)
flowers.wildlife: Goldfinches eat seeds. Attracts native bees and butterflies.
flowers.description: Golden yellow daisy-like flowers on delicate ferny foliage. One of Georgia's most garden-worthy native wildflowers — extremely drought-tolerant, long-blooming, and attractive to wildlife. The official state wildflower of Florida as well. Very adaptable to dry, poor soil conditions.

flowers.name: Wild Azalea (Florida Flame)
flowers.habitat: Woodland streams, ravine slopes — Coastal Plain and Piedmont
flowers.wildlife: Important early-season nectar source for bumblebees and hummingbirds.
flowers.description: Fragrant orange-yellow azalea flowers that appear before the leaves — one of the earliest flowering shrubs in Georgia's woodland. Found along streams and ravine slopes in the Coastal Plain and Piedmont. Intensely fragrant — can be smelled from 50+ feet away on warm spring days.

flowers.name: Blazing Star (Liatris)
flowers.wildlife: Essential Monarch butterfly and native bee plant.
flowers.description: Tall magenta-purple flower spikes that bloom from the top downward — unusual among spike flowers. One of the most important native plants for Monarch butterflies migrating through Georgia in fall. Also supports dozens of native bee species. Very easy to grow from corms.

flowers.name: Oakleaf Hydrangea
flowers.wildlife: Provides nesting structure. Attracts native bees.
flowers.description: Georgia's native hydrangea — spectacular large white flower clusters on a handsome shrub with distinctive oak-leaf-shaped leaves that turn brilliant burgundy-red in fall. Grows naturally along rocky stream banks in the Piedmont and mountains. Three seasons of interest: spectacular flowers, peeling cinnamon-colored bark, and exceptional fall color. One of the best native shrubs for the Southeast.

flowers.name: Purple Coneflower
flowers.wildlife: Goldfinches eat seeds. 50+ bee species. Monarch nectar.
flowers.description: Native to Georgia's open woodland and prairie clearings, purple coneflower provides critical late-summer nectar for Monarchs moving through Georgia on their fall migration to Mexico. Goldfinches feed on the seed heads through winter, clinging acrobatically to the spiny cones. The roots have well-documented immune-boosting properties.

flowers.name: Indian Pink
flowers.wildlife: Hummingbird specialist — tubular red flowers. Rare woodland plant.
flowers.description: One of Georgia's most spectacular native wildflowers — brilliant red tubular flowers with yellow interiors on upright stems in rich woodland. The intense red color and tubular shape signal exclusive hummingbird pollination. Increasingly rare due to deer pressure and forest understory destruction. An outstanding native plant for shaded garden situations.

flowers.name: Needle Palm
flowers.habitat: Coastal plain hammocks, swamp edges — Georgia native
flowers.wildlife: Berries eaten by wildlife. Provides dense habitat structure.
flowers.description: The most cold-hardy palm in the world — native to Georgia's coastal plain hammocks and swamp edges, hardy to zone 6 with protection. Compact clumping growth with needle-like spines protecting the base. Small fruits eaten by wildlife. An extraordinary plant — a true palm that can survive below-zero temperatures. Increasingly used in cold-hardy tropical garden designs.

flowers.name: Swamp Rose Mallow
flowers.habitat: Freshwater marshes, pond margins, tidal wetlands
flowers.wildlife: Specialist native bees. Important wetland plant.
flowers.description: Enormous native hibiscus with dinner-plate-sized pink to white flowers rising from Georgia's freshwater marshes and pond edges. Among the largest flowers of any native plant in the eastern US. Specialist native bees in the genus Ptilothrix evolved specifically to collect pollen from native Hibiscus — these bees depend entirely on this plant for survival.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Orange Blossom
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full plant entry for ecological details.
flowers.description: Florida's state flower — the intensely fragrant white blossoms of Florida's orange groves.

flowers.name: Coreopsis (Tickseed)
flowers.wildlife: Seeds eaten by birds. Attracts native bees and butterflies.
flowers.description: Florida's state wildflower — golden yellow daisy-like flowers that bloom year-round along roadsides and in wet prairies. Florida has planted millions of tickseed seeds along its highways since the 1990s, creating spectacular golden roadside displays that have become iconic. One of Florida's most recognizable wildflowers.

flowers.name: Simpson's Stopper
flowers.habitat: Tropical hammocks, coastal woodland — South Florida
flowers.wildlife: Berries eaten by many bird species. Important tropical native shrub.
flowers.description: Fragrant white flowers and orange-red berries on an evergreen native shrub of South Florida's tropical hammocks. Provides year-round food for wildlife. One of the most important native plants for birds in South Florida. Often planted as a landscape shrub.

flowers.name: Swamp Lily
flowers.wildlife: Attracts sphinx moths (night pollination).
flowers.description: Spectacular fragrant white flowers on tall stems rising from freshwater swamps and pond edges across Florida. Blooms primarily at night, attracting sphinx moths as pollinators. Large strap-like leaves remain evergreen in frost-free zones. Among Florida's most dramatic native aquatic plants.

flowers.name: Spiderwort
flowers.wildlife: Attracts native bees. Pollen collected by specialist bees.
flowers.description: Deep purple-blue three-petaled flowers with fuzzy yellow stamens — one of Florida's most common and cheerful native wildflowers. Opens in the morning and closes by early afternoon. The sap turns pink-purple in response to pollution — used as a biomarker for radiation and other environmental stresses.

flowers.name: Coral Honeysuckle
flowers.habitat: Woodland edges, fence rows, open forest
flowers.wildlife: Essential Ruby-throated Hummingbird vine. Berries eaten by thrushes.
flowers.description: Native coral-red tubular honeysuckle — far superior to the invasive Japanese honeysuckle for wildlife. The tubular red flowers are perfectly designed for Ruby-throated Hummingbird pollination. Not fragrant like the invasive species — the scent was traded for hummingbird specialization. Evergreen in mild winters.

flowers.name: Wild Canna
flowers.habitat: Freshwater marshes, wet ditches, pond margins
flowers.wildlife: Attracts hummingbirds. Seeds eaten by waterfowl.
flowers.description: Florida's native canna lily — large bright yellow flowers on tall stems rising from freshwater marshes and wet roadside ditches. The ancestor of most cultivated canna hybrids. Provides spectacular tropical-looking color in wet garden spots. Hummingbirds visit the flowers; large seeds are eaten by waterfowl.

flowers.name: Firebush
flowers.wildlife: Essential hummingbird plant. Attracts butterflies. Berries for birds.
flowers.description: One of Florida's most wildlife-valuable native shrubs — clusters of orange-red tubular flowers attract both Ruby-throated and Rufous Hummingbirds plus butterflies continuously from spring to frost. The small dark berries feed dozens of bird species. Grows rapidly in Florida's heat and humidity. Semi-evergreen to evergreen in frost-free areas.

flowers.name: Muhly Grass
flowers.habitat: Dry sandy flatwoods, rocky outcrops, roadsides
flowers.wildlife: Seeds eaten by ground-feeding birds. Habitat structure.
flowers.description: Florida's spectacular fall show plant — airy pink-purple seedhead clouds covering dry sandy areas and rocky outcrops each fall. One of the most photographed native plants in Florida. Florida's highway department plants millions each year along roadsides for spectacular fall displays. Extremely drought-tolerant once established. Native to the coastal plain from Florida to Texas.

flowers.name: Saw Palmetto
flowers.habitat: Sandhills, flatwoods, coastal scrub — Florida dominant
flowers.wildlife: Berries eaten by 100+ species. Critical Florida wildlife plant.
flowers.description: The defining plant of Florida's landscape — saw palmetto covers vast areas of the state's sandhills, flatwoods, and coastal scrub. Despite being a palm, it typically stays low and spreading rather than developing a trunk. The berries are eaten by over 100 wildlife species including Florida black bears, scrub jays, and gopher tortoises. The berries also support a multi-million dollar supplement industry.

flowers.name: Fringed Neottia
flowers.habitat: Dry longleaf pine savanna — Florida endemic
flowers.wildlife: Specialist orchid of fire-maintained habitats.
flowers.description: A rare native terrestrial orchid of Florida's dry longleaf pine savanna — greenish-brown flowers are inconspicuous but ecologically fascinating. Depends entirely on periodic fire to maintain the open, sunny, low-competition habitat it requires. As longleaf pine savanna has declined by over 97%, this orchid has disappeared from most of its former range. Found primarily in the Florida panhandle.

flowers.name: Chapman's Butterwort
flowers.habitat: Wet savannas — extremely rare Florida endemic
flowers.wildlife: Carnivorous. Critical indicator of pristine wet savanna.
flowers.description: A rare carnivorous native of Florida's wet pine savannas — flat rosettes of pale green leaves covered with sticky glands that trap small insects. Purple flowers resembling small violets appear in late winter. Found only in a handful of locations in the Florida panhandle — one of the most endangered carnivorous plants in North America. An indicator of near-pristine savanna conditions.

flowers.name: Gopher Apple
flowers.habitat: Dry sandy scrub, longleaf pine flatwoods
flowers.wildlife: Critical food plant for gopher tortoise. Berries for many wildlife.
flowers.description: A low, spreading native shrub of Florida's dry sandy scrub and longleaf pine flatwoods — white flowers followed by white to pale yellow fruits that are a critical food source for the gopher tortoise (a federally threatened species). The relationship between gopher tortoise and gopher apple is a keystone ecological interaction — the tortoise disperses the seeds in its droppings. Many other scrub animals also rely on the fruit.
